question: We serve a patient who has just suffered a traffic accident. She is conscious and when taking the constants she has a systolic blood pressure of 70 mmHg and a heart rate of 45 beats / minute. In addition, the skin of the extremities is hot. What is the most likely cause of the shock?
analysis: The patient presents with hypotension (systolic blood pressure of 70 mmHg) and bradycardia (heart rate of 45 beats/min), along with warm extremities. These signs are indicative of neurogenic shock, which can occur after a traumatic injury, particularly if there is spinal cord involvement. In neurogenic shock, there is a loss of sympathetic tone leading to vasodilation and warm skin despite low blood pressure. Other types of shock, such as hypovolemic or cardiogenic, would typically present with cold, clammy skin due to peripheral vasoconstriction.
